Consideration of the motion of Mr. James Mclsaac for an address to His Excellency the Governor General, in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, resumed "from Tuesday, February 22.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the House, for I do not feel that I can add anything that would be of material benefit to what has already been so ably said by hon. members on this side of the House in connection with the important matters

that have been placed before us in the speech from the Throne.
First, I want to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address upon the very able manner in which they performed that duty. I would also like to say a few words in connection with the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). In listening to the speeches of hon. members opposite, and especially the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) when he spoke of the wonderful leadership of the leader of the Opposition, who is going to blaze the way to greater things, as I am a labour man and one who was very closely associated with the Grand Trunk railway employees who went out on strike in 1910, my mind naturally went back to that time, and also to the famous resolution which was presented to the House last year by the leader of the Opposition, which is almost the same as the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition at this session, and now before the House for discussion. Mr. Speaker, I believe that the leader of the Opposition was just as insincere last year when he moved that famous resolution as he is this year in moving the amendment, and as he was when he promised the Grand Trunk Railway employees their positions back in 1910. The leader of the Opposition was Minister of Labour when the Grand Trunk strike occurred and as Minister of Labour he attempted to arbitrate between the company and the men, and after the strike had lasted for several days, on the assurance of the then Minister of Labour that the men would receive their positions back, or in other words, be reinstated in good standing, the strike was called off. And what were the results? We all know too well. Many of the men were never taken back, and many that were taken back did not receive their seniority standing. Apparently the now leader of the Opposition either betrayed the men or he did not have the ability to negotiate a proper settlement. In any event, he did not live up to his promises that if the men called off the strike he would accept the responsibility of seeing that the men got their positions back, as was the basis of the negotiations and settlement. I am informed that one of his party has been heard to remark that when the Opposition defeats the Government and the now leader of the Opposition becomes the leader of the Government, the Grand Trunk men will receive their pensions. As a matter of fact, the

only Grand Trunk employees who are not now receiving their pensions are those who failed in obtaining reinstatement by reason of the breaking of the promise given by the present leader of the Opposition. Had he at that time kept faith the pension dispute would never have arisen.
It is to be observed that the present Administration has done everything to facilitate a prompt and proper adjustment of the claims of these ex-employees, by placing in the hands of their solicitor all the information available in the files of the Department of Labour, and it has agreed that they shall have the opportunity to present their case as a claim against the Grand Trunk before the Board of Arbitration now sitting, and I have every confidence that justice will be done and that the men will receive their pensions.
Mr. Speaker, how do the issues now standing before the country affect the working man? The present Government stands for just such a measure of protection in our tariff system as will enable Canadian industries-agriculture, mining, lumbering and manufacturing-to continue to carry on to the greatest possible degree. The tariff proposals of the Opposition to the Government are that the protective principle must be eliminated; that industries that cannot meet the competition of the surplus products from the industries of the United States and the cheap labour of foreign countries must be sacrificed without any regard to what happens to the thousands of men that these industries employ. That, Mr. Speaker, I think you will agree, is a fair statement of the issufe as it is presented to us.
Well, Sir, how is that going to affect the wage-earner? The industries of the province of Ontario employ around around four hundred thousand men. They use large quantities of raw material produced by other Canadian workingmen. They furnish traffic to our railways and employment to our railwaymen. They provide markets for our farmers and business for our business men. Every industry added to those we now have widens the opportunity and improves the conditions of our people. Every industry forced to close by unfair competition has just the opposite effect. How would it affect the workmen if in Ontario, for instance, the Westing-house Company, the Ford Motor Company, the United Typewriter Company, the Simonds Saw Company, the Yates Machine Company, and scores of other American
companies with branch factories in Canada, closed their doors and furnished the Canadian market from their American plants? Yet, Mr. Speaker, the only thing that is keeping these industries in Canada is a moderate protective tariff. Every time the output from a Canadian industry is reduced or curtailed by the competition of imported goods, workingmen suffer. Every dollar's worth of goods imported into this country that could be legitimately produced here means taking the bread and butter from some Canadian working man's child. And yet we have public men going about this country preaching the doctrines of class warfare, with one object, and one object alone-the hope that they may enlist the support of workingmen in a movement destined to destroy their chances of earning a decent livlihood.
There is another question that has not been touched upon by many o' the previous speakers, and it is one in which I am deeply interested. It is the investigation that is being conducted by the Department of Labour into a system of unemployment insurance and old age pensions. On account of being a labour man, I1 perhaps know a great deal more of the actual conditions of the workingman than the majority of the members of the House, and I also feel I am in a better position to know just about how much the labourer can save out of his earnings after he properly cares for his family. Unemployment may arise from other causes than the loss of position. A man may become unemployed through sickness, invalidity or old age. Very few labourers are able to make provision for these contingencies and the question of making some provision by a system of state social insurance for those who through no fault of their own are unable to work whether the inability arises from lack of opportunity, sickness, invalidity, or old age is of very great importance. Such insurance would remove the, spectre of fear which now haunts the wage earner, and would make him a more contented and better citizen. I have in mind at this time, labouring men who were strong and robust when the war broke out. They were too old to go to the front, but I know for a fact that they contributed every dollar they could spare to help along the good work. Sickness has overtaken them, and they are to-day down and out, through no fault of their own. These men might have saved money had they not been so generous, but they felt

that as true Canadians they had a duty; not being able to fight themselves, they helped in every way possible the men who were fighting for them. I hope that the department's investigation will be carried on, and that we may be successful in having legislation placed upon the statute books at this session of Parliament, providing insurance of this character.
Mr. Speaker, what has made this possible, and what has this Government done for labour? The Minister of Labour, who himself was a labour man, was appointed by this Government, and he has shown to the people of Canada that he is worthy of the honourable position he now holds. In 1919 the Government of Canada established a Royal Commission presided over by Chief Justice Mathers of Winnipeg, whose duty it was to inquire into and take evidence respecting industrial conditions in Canada. Following their report, the Department of Labour invited to a conference a substantial number of representative employers and of organized labour throughout Canada, with representatives from each of the Provincial Governments. This body after going fully into the report of the Mathers Commission, appointed a committee - composed of representatives of employers and of labour. This committee endorsed the recommendation of the Mathers Commission and suggested that a careful investigation of the whole subject should be undertaken. This was done, and I am informed that our Department of Labour has been making a careful investigation and has gathered a large amount of useful information from all countries in the world that have adopted, or contemplate adopting, legislation on unemployment insurance. I am further informed that the information so gathered is being submitted to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and to the Trades and Labor Congress of Canada, which organizations are the principal representatives of employers and employees in this country. I therefore think the .Government of Canada is to be complimented upon the sane, careful methods which it has adopted in co-operation with those most intimately concerned, and that this House, may without hesitation, give hearty approval and endorsement to that portion of the speech from the Throne which indicates the policy of the Government in connection with these two most important questions, which, if solved, will tend more to stabilize industry, promote peace, and make happy citizens than anything else that could be done.
(I Mr. Harrison.]

speakeroldname: Mr. MARIE JOSEPH DEMERS (St. Johns and Iberville) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to my judgment, the political atmosphere in which we live at present does not make very long speeches desirable, and I do not feel disposed to take up very much time in the remarks I have to make this afternoon. I intend to confine myself to one or two salient observations. Following an old and very appropriate custom, and emulating the example of these who have spoken before me, may I be permitted to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address on the able speches they delivered, which were in accordance with the best traditions of this House. It is hardly necessary, I fancy, to say that although I appreciate the oratorical ability of those two gentlemen I am very far from sharing in their appreciation of, and admiration for this Government.
If the newspapers are to be believed, the result of the election in Peterborough has thrown disorder, discomfort, and even confusion into the ranks of the Government to such an extent that we can expect anything at any time. This session may last three weeks, perhaps a month, perhaps longer; no one knows. Uncertainty is the state of mind of everybody at the presen* time, and I want to ask you this question, Mr. Speaker:	Under present circumstances do you believe that the members of this House should have been summoned to meet here? Is this a proper time to begin session, and can we expect anything substantial as a result of our deliberations? This government* apparently ignores the lessons of history. I am pretty sure that history will repeat itself, and it seems to me that it is unnecessary for one to have a very long political experience in order to foresee the general election which is inevitable in the near future. The government say " No" to this, but to my mind their negative assertions have no signifance whatever. Laws of nature, if I may say so, are above the will and the desire of any government. There is, in the situation with which we are confronted, something that is unprecedented, and that is the unanimity of the newspapers friendly to the Government in admitting the weakness of this Administration and advising it to give up without further ado. I think that the attitude of the newspapers friendly to the Government, after the election in Peterborough, was something unique, and the weakness of this Government must be very apparent since it is freely admitted even by its best friends. Under such circumstances, there-

fore, I cannot believe that this Government will not understand at last that its duty is undoubtedly indicated. Everyone is looking for a general election, even its best friends. Let us, therefore, have an election. Let the government give up that old bluff which they have paraded on so many occasions and which certain newspapers are meanly repeating, to the effect that even the Liberal Opposition does not favour a general election at the present time.
I do not believe that there is another example in the history of this country of a government so much discredited and disliked as the present administration. But there is a reason for that. We should keep in mind the fact that this is the first time that we have had in this country a government of usurpers. This expression, I know, has frequently been used lately, but I think it is very appropriate. The Administration, so far as I can see, will go down with humiliation and it will deserve-to use the expressive popular phrase-" what is coming to it."
Let us remember under what circiimr stances the Unionist Government was formed. A certain group of Liberal members decided to sever their connections with their leader on account of the war because they differed with him as to the nature of the contribution that Canada should make to the conduct of the war. They joined the Government of the day. But although they retired from their party, they solemnly declared that their retirement was but temporary, and they asserted emphatically that Liberals they were and Liberals they would remain, and that as soon as the war was over they would return to their party and stand by its principles and ideals. Some of them were men of conviction and sincerity; they fulfilled their promise and came back to their party. But, Mr. Speaker, what can we say of those who concluded a permanent alliance with their new friends on the strength of nothing better or more plausible than the motto: "What we have we hold?" Are the attractions of power then so strong? The election of 1917 was held under exceptional circumstances and under abnormal conditions. It was a war-time election conducted under a war-time electoral law. The platform of the Unionist party contained only one plank, "Win the War," and that war-cry was intended to appeal to every one irrespective of political affiliations. Some special and most extraordinary laws were passed in order to give the right to vote even to foreigners and
to deprive some citizens of this country of the same right. There was a special selection of electors, and the law was so framed as to permit the manipulation of ballots, and naturally that law was put into practice by means of cipher and other devices, with this result, that many of the hon. members sitting in this House are not the choice of the residents of the ridings they are supposed to represent. And I cannot give a better example, a more palpable and striking example, than the hon. gentleman who spoke before me. I have here the Canadian Parliamentary Guide and according to it these were the votes cast in the constituency of Nipissing at the last election:	Harrison, 4,879
Lapierre, 6,218. About thirteen hundred votes for the hon. gentleman were found outside of the riding and he was declared elected by a majority of forty-four.
Shame.

Proceeding, Mr. Speaker, to consider the circumstances under which the election of 1917 was conducted, let me say that a large number of votes, especially in Ontario, were obtained under false pretences, and it seems to me that under such circumstances it is impossible for a man of ordinary intelligence not to perceive the exceptional character of such an election, its temporary character, and the necessity for another general election at the earliest possible date after the war. The Government have failed to appreciate that fact, and that is the principal reason for the unrest which exists in this country and which manifests itself at every opportunity. Mr. Speaker, there can be no relief from the situation until constitutional government is restored-that is to say as long as the people of Canada are not satisfied that they have a government which has their confidence and which is supported by a majority of regularly chosen representatives. This satisfaction the people naturally cannot obtain except through a general election.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, during his political journey throughout the country, was naturally very generous and very charitable. He described his opponents of all classes as Bolsheviki, disturbers, dangerous and disloyal elements, and indulged in other similar moderate epithets, but, Mr. Speaker, I am very' sure that all those who are listening to the Prime Minister-

I think the Prime Minister should address his reproach to the newspapers. I am pretty sure, Mr. Speaker, that when the Prime Minister was speaking about Bolsheviki, disturbers, and all such elements, the great majority of his hearers thought he was trying to give an adequate description of the group over which he presides. Because all those who were listening to the Prime Minister knew that throughout its whole life his administration has evidenced a continued contempt for order and for constitutional rule. His administration has been, and still is, the reign of arbitrary authority. Why should we recapitulate what is well known? When I speak about the Government I am referring to the administrations from 1914 to date, without any distinction between them, because even if it is true that the visible head of the previous government has disappeared we feel that the spirit is still there and more formidable than ever since it is more intimately associated than ever with the visible head of the present Administration. Let me say in passing that nothing was less surprising to me than the appointment of the right hon. gentleman to the position of Prime Minister of Canada. It was only what we might have expected. This nomination is absolutely in accordance with the evidence of the last seven years. Nevertheless I -must say that it is a nomination which is keenly resented by a large section of the people of the Dominion. Personally, when everybody is urging the necessity of unity and harmony in this country I think there could not be a worse move than the appointment to the office of Prime Minister of a man who will always be an element of division and dissension. Do not ask me why. The Prime Minister speaking about Quebec said somewhere that he had never uttered a word against that province. Would he swea'r to that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
He would not dare to . do it.

Let me tell the Prime Minister that in Quebec, as in other provinces, words have less importance than facts and doings; the first minister must deem us very credulous when he comes and asks the question "Who can say that 1 ever uttered a word against Quebec?" The Prime Minister says he never said a word against Quebec.
Hear, hear.

Sir, the right hon. gentleman knows that Quebec does not like him. He said so when in the province last year. How does he know that, since, accord ing to his own conscience, there is no justification at all for the attitude of hostility towards him on the part of Quebec? Die anybody tell him that, or is it only an impression of his? Let me inform the Prime Minister that his psychological appreciation of the attitude of Quebec against him is correct, and he should be the last man to come and ask why? In my opinion such an attitude on his part is an aggravation of the offence. Let me tell him that in Quebec, while we can easily forgive and forget words, we forgive but never forget facts. At all events I am sure that I represent the sentiments of the people of that province when I say that we are waiting for an election and when the time comes the people of Quebec will do their share, in conjunction with the people of the other provinces of Canada, in overthrowing this Government.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I should restrict myself to the question of the necessity of a general election, for that is the only question of interest to our people, and undoubtedly they all desire a general election.
Except the Government.

No one class of the population is satisfied with this Administration. Look at the farmers, the returned soldiers, the working men, the consumers-among one and all of them you will find the same dissatisfaction. On the restoration of peace there was necessity in this country, as in the other belligerent countries, for rigid economy and a ruthless cutting down of the expenses of administration. What happened. We entered into the policy of public ownership-proved to be disastrous

everywhere else; we became shipbuilders; we increased our military expenditure by two-thirds over what it had been under prewar conditions; we organized a very expensive navy, without any occasion for it;
and as far as the expenses of the
3	p.m. League of Nations are concerned, we are told to-day that Canada is considered one of the greatest powers of the world, and the Government is satisfied with its work. But, Mr. Speaker, what could we expect of a Government which has been acustomed to uncontrolled extravagance and waste during a period of four years and a half of warfare? This is one of the obvious reasons why the Government should have understood that it was its duty to limit its activity strictly to the purposes for which it had been chosen.
We are told that there will be an Imperial Conference in London this year. In that connection I want to ask this question: Who ever received a mandate from the people to go to that Conference and speak for Canada? And who will have the audacity to go there and speak for us?
To my mind, Sir, the Government by its continuance in office is assuming a terrible and dangerous responsibility, and I am pretty sure that when the time comes it will realize the extent of the anger of the people.

Before applying myself to the important questions mentioned in His Excellency's speech, I should like to offer my congratulations to the hon. gentleman who so acceptably moved the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the Throne. I congratulate the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Mclsaac) on the very eloquent literary contribution he made to the pages of Hansard. It does him credit, and it reflects honour upon his constituents who are responsible for his presence in this House. I trust that the hon. gentleman may survive the vicissitudes of the next election in order to come back here and tell hon. members more about the sounding sea and the thunder of its surf. I would also compliment the hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) on the very excellent maiden speech which he delivered in seconding the motion. He well merits the very many complimentary remarks showered upon him by hon. members from both sides of the House. He has a clear, resonant voice and an ability to marshal his facts so that they carry conviction. He bears the impress of a polished speaker, and we welcome him here as a decided addition to the debating powers of this assembly.
I would be remiss in my duty as a member of Parliament and a Canadian did I not give some expression of my deep appreciation of the great services rendered to Canada and to the Empire by the illustrious gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) who so recently relinquished the office of Prime Minister. I am one of those-and the number is large-who believe that men are raised up by Providence to guide the destinies of a people in the hour of their dire distress and danger. It was by no mere accident or blind chance that our ex-Prime Minister was returned as leader of the Government in the election of 1911. It was by no mere accident or through no blind chance that the ministry of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier appealed to the country in the mid-period of their parliamentary term in the expectation of getting a snatch victory at the polls. Hon. gentlemen opposite may not agree with me in seeing the hand of Providence in that event; they will probably say that it was an instance of the great statesmanlike powers and political foresight of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). But the ex-Prime Minister was the one man in Canada possessed of the

intellectual attainments, the prophetic vision, the determination of purpose necessary to the guiding of this country through the intricacies of international diplomacy during the war. He was the one man in Canada possessed of the qualities of head and heart and body to enable him to withstand the great mental and physical strain during that conflict, to bear up under the tremendously increased burdens of state, and to stay in harness until the victory was won. I regret as much as any man can regret the disability which compelled him to retire. The Canadian people may not be willing to accord to him that measure of honour to which his great services justly entitle him, but I have confidence that the future historian, in summing up the achievements of the war, will accord to Sir Robert Borden a foremost place amongst the great statesmen of the British Empire.
Prime Ministers come and Prime Ministers go; long live our Prime Minister. I offer my heartiest congratulations to the present leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) on his elevation to the highest position in the gift of the Canadian people. He was selected on account of his personal charm and his commanding ability as a Parliamentarian. He is a real statesman and will give a good account of his stewardship to the people of this country. Since Confederation we have been blessed with good Prime Ministers. I am speaking now without regard to politics; a man's politics have nothing more to do with his attributes as a man than his religious creed has to do with his qualities as a Christian-the qualities are inherent in the man himself. The hon. Alexander Mackenzie, Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson and Sir Wilfrid Laurier were all men of high ideals, of great executive ability, and of unimpeachable charater. Our present Prime Minister will rank high when compared with these men; he will do honour to the Canadian people while receiving honour at their hands.
In considering the speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, I was struck by the many important issues mentioned there as the basis of proposed legislation at this session of Parliament. In that connection I would like to make a few remarks with regard to the speech made by the leader of the Opposition. I must say that I was disappointed in that speech; it was not worthy of the leader of a great party aspiring to the Premiership of this great country. He failed, in his two hours' fusillade delivered with the speed of

a quick-firing maxim gun, to touch upon one of the subjects mentioned in His Excellency's speech. He had no criticism to offer of the record of the Government and of the policy as laid down. Assuming that silence gives assent, we must say that the hon. leader of the Opposition is in accord with the policies and with the record of the Government.
. On the -first page of the speech from the Throne I find a reference to the prosperity of the Canadian people, the general unrest throughout the country and the world and the contraction of business, and also a reference to taxes. These questions are apparently of no importance to the leader of the Opposition; they sink into insignificance when compared with his own ambition to be leader of the Government. On the second page we find mention of the unemployment situation-that it is worldwide. Mr. Speaker, the unemployment at the present time-and I am speaking now with regard to my own section of the country-is no greater than it was in the winter of 1914 and in preceding winters. On account of the material prosperity which the people enjoyed during the war, most of the labour sections were able to take care of themselves out of the savings which they had laid by during that period.
I am willing to admit that there are men who, through circumstances over which they had no control, have found it difficult to obtain the necessaries of life for themselves and for their families. There are others, however, who live up to all they can make, no matter how much it is; who have no idea of thrift, and who are always in want if they are not at work. A system has been instituted under which, through the assistance of local governments and municipalities, these people can get relief.
Reference is made in the speech from the Throne to the matter of unemployment insurance. I compliment the Government on its courage in bringing this question up. I look upon it as a rather dangerous question and one that must be carefully looked into. Any action taken in that regard must be surrounded by every possible_ safeguard. A system of unemployment insurance might be easily abused; if a good Act is not brought in, the result might be the discouragement of thrift and the encouragement of indolence. I would have thought that the leader of the Opposition, who has studied labour questions and who poses as an expert in these matters, would be able to give some useful and constructive suggestions to the Government with regard to
this important question, particularly in view of the fact that he must have gained some useful information while in the United States during the period of the war, at a time when our Government was sweating blood, one might say, in an effort to save this country for future generations. But did the hon. gentleman even mention the subject? No. Mr. Speaker, it was of no importance; he brushed it aside as he would the dust from his desk. He has no interest whatever in the trials of the working people, in their efforts to gain a livelihood and to keep their wives and children in comfort during the time of unemployment.
The next question, which is a very important subject and one that must be handled with gloves, is that of Old Age Pensions, and I again compliment the Government on its courage in bringing this matter before Parliament. It must be handled carefully, as it is a subject that may be very easily abused if legislation should be enacted. There are many people who are not able to take care of themselves and who have not sufficient saved from their earnings to take care of them in their old age, so that such legislation is probably necessary, although there are other countries in which it is more necessary than in this great country of Canada where everyone has an equal chance and there is every opportunity for people to make a living and save. This question, however, is an important one; the Government is investigating it, and it will be brought before Parliament at this session.
Yet it also is brushed aside by the leader of the Opposition as a matter of no importance; it pales into insignificance when compared with his ambition to be Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada. In his speech, he said that the question of the mandate of the Government transcended in importance all other questions; that until it was settled, questions of lesser importance would need be delayed, and,all the subjects mentioned in the Speech from the Throne are regarded by him as being of less importance than his personal interests. Was there ever such a statement made by a leader of the Opposition in any Parliament of the world, that he placed his personal interests above tjie interests of the people and the State?
Another question of great interest to the people of this country is in regard to the League of Nations. The representatives sent by Canada to the Assembly of the League have already spoken on that

question, and I wish to compliment those gentlemen upon the very excellent way in which they looked after the interests of Canada and, indeed, of the American continent. They deserve the praiseworthy remarks made of their actions by the people of the United States. They Were, one might say, the spokesmen of the whole American continent; they held the name of Canada high in the councils of the world, and they gained for themselves a very enviable international reputation.
We come to the consideration of the tariff, the revision of the tariff, that question which was of so much importance last year, but which, according to my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King), is of no importance rfow. The leader of the Opposition, at a meeting held in Milton in August of last year, made an appeal to the people and particularly to the farmers. He mentioned on that occasion that his fiscal policy was a tariff for the producer and the consumer. I wonder if any gentleman on either side of the House can tell us what that really means. I am quite satisfied that the audience to which he was speaking in the county of Halton did not understand it. It was a statement made purposely to mislead. He had with him, in order to convey two impressions to the people, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and everybody knows what the hon. member stands for with regard to a fiscal policy. The leader of the Opposition said:
It is not a question of free trade or protection. It is a tariff for consumers) and producers.
The leader of the Opposition intended to convey two ideas to the people of that county. Like Santa Claus at Christmas, he had something for everybody. The leader of the Opposition is the greatest political Santa Claus this country has ever had. To those people who were inclined to favour protection or low tariff, he said: "Here, you can have protection; you can have a moderate tariff; this is a tariff for consumers and producers." The hon. member for Brome could give the impression to the free traders that this meant free trade, and consequently everybody should be pleased and should vote for the hon. member for Brome and his leader. That did not quite satisfy the audience, because he was speaking to hard-headed Scotchmen, Englishmen and Irishmen by whom that county is settled, the descendants of men who came from the old land many generations ago. They were not easily carried away by the piffle which the leader of the 
Opposition gave them-it did not go down and it was not long afterwards that the hon. member for Brome was asked to return and explain the conditions and the position. He went to the town of Oakville, a short distance from Milton and made a speech there. That speech was not reported in the press so that I did not hear what he said; but I heard that the hon. member travelled something like 400 miles to address an audience of fifty people. My hon. friend can corroborate that, as he is in a better position than I to know whether it is true or not. I might say that the speech delivered at Milton by the leader of the Opposition was practically the same as the speeches he delivered at Newmarket and Toronto; he has it off by heart; he can stand up in this House and it will go off of its own volition. He said, speaking in Toronto on the 16th of August last:
We have ini Ottawa, as we hadi in this province, a Government which has undertaken to perpetuate itself in office without any reference whatever to the wishes of the people, or without permitting any expression of the popular will.
He means to say that the Government of Sir William Hearst was perpetuating itself in office without asking the will of the people. We know that he did stay a little longer in office on account of the conditions of the war, but that was by unanimous consent of both parties in the legislature. He was not using autocratic power any more than we are in Ottawa. But the leader of the Opposition continued:
We have neither a representative Parliament nor a responsible Government. We have an autocratie executive usurping authority, exercising political control, regardless alike of constitutional procedure and the first principles of Government in a free and self-groveming- country.
I think few men in the Dominion of Canada will deny that Canada is a free and self-governing country, and there are in the Dominion not many men who will say to-day that the present Government is exercising autocratic power. That is something that exists only in the mind of the leader of the Opposition and his followers, and they have reiterated it so often that they have commenced to believe it. The leader of the Opposition, in stating his position with regard to the resignation of the Government, did so with such vehemence and show of indignation that I was almost persuaded that he meant what he said, but in listening to his followers afterwards I came to the conclusion that he was not sincere in his demand.

Why should he he? At Milton he made an appeal to the farmers and frankly stated:	We, myself and the Liberal party,
cannot possibly defeat this Government, and we ask an alliance with the farmers, the labour men and the returned soldiers to assist us in turning out this Government. Mr. Speaker, what would an alliance with the Agrarian party mean? The leader of the Opposition has a tariff for the producer and the consumer, and if he goes to the country he has no hope of returning here with a majority sufficient to enable him to carry on without the support of the Agrarian party to his left. What would that mean? Would it mean that if the leader of the Opposition became the leader of the Government we would have a tariff for the producer and tihe consumer? If he has the assistance of the Agrarian group in forming a 'government in order to carry on, it will mean free trade, nothing more or less. He would be compelled to accede to the wishes of the leader of the Agrarian party, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who is frankly an out-and-out free trader.
I do not think the hon. gentleman will deny it. I do not see him in the House at this moment, but I have here a couple of clippings from speeches he made in the West, which I think will be quite conclusive that he is a free trader. Speaking at a convention of the United Farmers of Alberta on January 26, 1920, he is reported by the Grain Growers' Guide of February 11, 1920, to have said (pp. 56-59) :
Now the farmers of this country, by pronouncing upon the Questions, have stated their belief that the principle of protection is not only economically unsijund but morally indefensible, is it not time we were considering a change in regard to it?
Then in his speech of November 19, 1919, as reported in the issue of the Regina Leader of November 20, Mr. Crerar said:
If people want to wear diamonds and silks and have the money for it, at this stage of our country's advancement, I have no objection to it, but I do say this: that if we.tax them with a customs tariff we must levy an excise tax on the home manufacturers. I would absolutely root out the principle of protection in our customs tariff.
Surely the leader of the Agrarian party will not deny what he said on those two occasions. He is frankly a free trader, and if the leader of the Opposition is returned without sufficient majority to carry on, and must depend upon the support given him by the Agrarian group to form a government, we must have
free trade. The hon. member for Marquette could not possibly deny the western provinces what they have been asking for, and the policy upon which they have returned him to this House. If he did, he would betray the farmers of the West, he would lose his position in the Grain Growers Grain Company, and would have to withdraw himself from the political life of Canada forever. So he would stand firmly by the principle of free trade, and the leader of the Opposition is paving the way by which he can grant free trade to this country if such a condition should arise. He wants to be able to say to the people of Canada: I have carried out my pre-election promises. Did I not tell you it would be a tariff for the consumer and the producer? Of course, that is a free trade tariff.
The leader of the Opposition has taken a good deal of comfort out of the results of the by-election in West Peterborugh. I might say he has been cackling over that one victory like a chicken over its first egg. Was there ever such an egg. Was there ever such a victory? The hon. gentleman's supporter who was elected in West Peterborough is not yet in this House, but he will come here as a minority candidate. He was elected by about one-third of the vote of that constituency. If that election tells us anything,'it tells us of the futility of the multiplicity of candidates and of what I might call the group system of government. Otherwise it tells us practically nothing. The Government had a majority of the votes cast in endorsation of their fiscal policy, but the leader of the Opposition says that that was not an issue in that election or in any other by-election. He says that the only issue is the mandate of the Government.
At nearly all the meetings the leader of the Opposition has addressed throughout the Dominion, he has dwelt very much upon what you might call his Liberalism. It is almost a religious faith with the hon. gentleman. He harps back to the old days of Liberalism many years ago, when Liberalism really meant something, when it really had some principles behind it; but it has no principles behind it to-day under the leadership of the hon. gentleman. He has evidently forgotten that the principles of Liberalism which he announces to-day in this House are nothing else but a moth-eaten bunch of contradictions, inconsistencies, and deceit. The hon. gentleman has really missed his calling. He might pose as a first-class actor in a dime museum. He

could pose with a wig and beard as Ananias, and if he poses as well as he acts the part, he will be a success.
The Liberals on this side of the House did not leave their party; they took their party with them when they crossed the floor. On more than one occasion the Liberals on this side of the House have been invited to recross the floor and take up their old allegiance. We had an invitation a few days ago from the hon. member for Brome, handed out in a fine manner. That versatile gentleman can do it very well indeed. Then, in 1918, we had an invitation from the leader of the Opposition of that day (Mr. McKenzie), when he announced to this House and to the followers who had wandered away from the camp that the light was in the window and the latch string on the outside of the door. That light, Mr. Speaker, may be designated the light that failed.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice) :
speechtext: A good many came back.

One or two political moths were attracted by the light, but the great majority of the Liberal Unionists who seceded from this side of the House have camped upon the trail uncertain whether to proceed or build a shack of their own. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) now looks very critically at the meagre fare spread in the Liberal kitchen, and has decided along with his followers to stay where they are until their own provisions are exhausted. They may then gradually go on into the Liberal camp.
The "mandate of the Government." It was the great theme of the address of the leader of the Opposition. What is a mandate anyway? Is it something you can eat that it should be exhausted so soon? The members of the Opposition must be famishing for something from the Government benches or they would not ask the question so often and reiterate it over and over again. There is constitutional authority for the conduct of this Government. If you consult the British North America Act of 1867 you will find, in section 50, ample constitutional authority for this or any other Government of this Dominion of Canada to take charge of the affairs of the country for a period of five years unless previously dissolved by the Governor-General. That is the only clause with regard to the constitutional authority of Parliament to sit for five years. The lea-

der of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned in his speech in Toronto that if there was constitutional authority for the Government of 1911 to proceed to the country, the same authority could now be invoked by this Government. Any one will admit that; but there was no necessity for the Government of 1911 to go to the country; they were not compelled to do so. They went of their own volition, thinking they would secure a record vote from the people. But the people did not support them in their contention; they voted strongly against them at the time, showing clearly that they did not look favourably upon the policy which the government was then advocating.
In section 51, sub-section 5, it is provided that every ten years a census shall be taken and a redistribution made every decade after the year 1871, which redistribution shall be made by the Parliament then constituted and shall take effect when the term of that Parliament expires. If the leader of the Government should accede to the demand, of the Opposition and go to the country at this time, redistribution could not take place before the expiration of the term of the Parliament then elected and would consequently be delayed for five years. As the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has so well pointed out, representation would then be denied the people in Western Canada and in such other territories where they are entitled to greater representation than they have at present.
Any Government that could be guilty of such an act and return here in violation of the principles of the British North America Act would, in very truth, be usurpers. It would be an autocratic act to prevent the people of Western and Eastern Canada from securing until the expiration of five years, after the date of the following election, the greater representation to which they are entitled. I do not believe that the leader of the Opposition can be sincere in his declarations; otherwise he would not take such a stand. If it should happen that the Government were forced to the country by the Opposition, the papers in Canada would not care to print what the Western people would say, for it would not be printable.
Now, with regard to the question of mandates. If the Government has a mandate, then the individual members of parliament have mandates also. In 1917 every member elected to support the Government had a mandate from the people to support the Unionist Administration not only during the

war but until the termination of the parliamentary period. Undoubtedly, the war was the main issue. There is no denying that fact. But it is news to me to hear the leader of the Opposition state that when the war was over it was incumbent on the Government to go to the country. I fought in that election, and I never heard the statement made, nor did it ever occur to me, that I was elected only for the period of the war. No one knew how long the war would last; no one knew how soon it would be concluded victoriously to the allies; and it was therefore absolutely impossible to say that the people of the country intended that the Government should hold office only for the period of the war. Nothing was further from their minds than such a supposition.
A mandate from the people is a command to do something; it is an order from the people for the Government to carry out its platform submitted to them. This Government has proceeded to do so, and to bring to fruition all the aims and objectives outlined in their platform; and I doubt whether there ever was a Government at Ottawa that more faithfully performed its duty in that respect. As I have said, every individual member elected to support the Unionist party had a .mandate from his constituency to support the Government so long as it remained in office.
Hon. gentlemen who have seceded from this side and gone across the floor could take only one honourable stand. When they did not see eye to eye with their constituents, when they decided to abandon their allegiance to the present Government and cross to the side benches, they should have resigned their seats and obtained a new mandate from the people. They are the ones that are betraying the people, and not the Government. The hon. member for Marquette (Hon. Mr. Crerar) was the greatest sinner in this respect. He practically started a trek across the road, and it was his duty, as leader of the Agrarian party, to go back to his constituents and ask them for a new mandate, and confirmation of the position he has taken as leader of that party across the floor.
What does the Liberal party care for mandates? Let us go back to the election of 1896. The late Laurier administration, on the issue of tariff for revenue only, appealed to the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other and circularized them continuously throughout the election for support on that issue, promising that if they were returned to power they would abolish the protective policy and give to the people a tariff for revenue purposes only. They were elected on that issue; they received a mandate from the people to put that policy into effect. Did they do so? , Mr. Speaker, history tells us that they did not; nevertheless they did not resign. Did they receive any mandate from the people of Canada to keep a protective policy in force in this country? They did not; yet in spite of that they remained in office for fifteen years, violating the first principles, according to their own views, of democratic institutions. And now they have the temerity to charge this Government, which is carrying out faithfully and fully its mandate received from the people, with usurpation of democratic power.
The hon. members of the Opposition have a great respect for the memory of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier; so have I. I regarded him as a great Canadian, a great statesman, and a man of unimpeachable character; and I think that what he said should have had some influence on the opinions of Opposition members with regard to the attitude they took in 1896. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Hon. Mr. Fielding), who is in his seat today, was Finance Minister of that Government and received a mandate from the people to wipe out the protective principle from the statute books and instead to institute a tariff for revenue only. But he refused to carry out the pledge of his party; he denied to the people the right they claimed and kept the protective policy in force.
Why did the hon. gentleman do so? With other members of the Government who were in office at that time he sounded the manufacturing interests, what are called the "big interests," and found that they would not stand for a reduction of the tariff. The then leader of the Government, with whom was associated the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) accordingly capitulated to those "big interests." And yet these hon. gentlemen have the audacity to say to-day that the present Government is controlled by the same big interests. Mr. Speaker, it is the greatest piffle that has ever been uttered in this House, and I am surprised at hon. gentlemen opposite occupying so much time in dilating upon such petty issues. They have been raising a clamour all through the country and during the present debate on
iREVISED EDITION

this question. Of course, we have always had clamourers but we should not take them too seriously. In 1833 there were such clamourers and, speaking in the Senate of the United States, Daniel Webster referred to them as follows:
There are persons who constantly clamor. They complain of oppression, and pernicious influence of accumulated' wealth. They cry out loudly against all banks and corporations and all means by which small capitalists become united in order to produce important and beneficial results. They carry on a mad hostility against all established institutions. They would choke the fountain of industry and dry all streams. In a country of unbounded liberty they clamor against oppression. In a country of perfect equality, they would move heaven and earth against privilege and monopoly. In a country where property is more evenly divided than anywhere else, they rend the air scouting agrarian doctrines. In a country where wages are high beyond parallel, they would teach the laborer that he is but an oppressed slave.
That was the dictum of Daniel Webster in 1833. We have such clamourers in the Dominion to-day and we will have them so long as Canada is in existence. In the course of time we shall have forgotten the clamourers of 1920 and 1921, but we will always remember those sane Canadians who stood firm in support of constituted authority and of a progressive administration of public affairs in the Dominion. The leader of the Opposition has the audacity to ask the Prime Minister by what right and by what warrant he intends to rule this country. I tell him that the Prime Minister and his Cabinet are ruling Canada by the warrant of the loyal Canadian citizens who stood faithfully by their country and fought for it day and night throughout four and a half years of the most stupendous conflict in the history of the world. By virtue of that right and that warrant they are entitled to the support of every man in this House, and they are entitled to the support of Canadians who stood shoulder to shoulder with the Government in conserving Canada to Canadians in order that the leader of the Opposition might have a country to come back to and that he might have the opportunity to assist in advancing the progress of this country throughout the years of peace which we hope are ahead of us.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman per-

mit me, please, for a moment? If the present time would be agreeable to the leader of the Opposition, I would like now to return to the order of Motions, with the consent of the House, so that we might take up the motion of which I gave notice on Tuesday. It occurred to me that possibly my hon. friend would otherwise take up the time between now and six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be proper for the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres to move the adjournment of the debate.

Very well, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move the adjournment of the Debate.	[DOT]
Motion agree to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg to move the Motion of which I gave notice on Tuesday, to the effect that the Order of the House making the debate on the Address the exclusive duty of the House until disposed of be varied to the extent of permitting Bill No. 2 to be proceeded with by this House to a conclusion. I have already given the House . the reasons why I make this motion. The necessity for this Bill being proceeded with is to enable its provisions to take effect in time to be put into operation so that it may be possible for the referendum to- be held in Ontario on the date fixed, and obviate any further necessity of its postponement. I want to explain, so that there will be no misunderstanding, that this could only be gone on -with, under the rules, by unanimous consent, but the leader of the Opposition not having seen his way, when I spoke to him last Friday to assure unanimous consent, I took the precaution to move to vary the rule. Consequently, I simply appear before the House asking that the Rule be varied by the will of the majority.

As my right hon. friend has said, the purpose of his motion is to enable the Government to proceed with the Bill which has come to this House from the Senate providing for an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act, 1919, so as to permit a referendum to be taken in the province of Ontario in the course of the next month or two at a less cost than would be involved if the vote were to be taken under the Elections Act as it stands at present. I think I am right in saying that if this Bill, which has come to us from the Senate, were not carried, its failure to pass would not prevent the referendum being taken; it would not lead, as my right hon. friend

intimated on Monday, to the disfranchisement of any person in the matter of that referendum, nor would it necessarily involve any delay in the taking of the referendum. All that it would involve would be an additional expense of some $300,000 in the cost of the preparation of the necessary lists.
As I interpret the circumstance it means that, through the lack of foresight on the part of the Government last session in anticipating a possibility of this kind, if the Bill does not pass the country will have to suffer an additional expense of $300,000. Now it is certainly not the desire of any of us on this side of the House to cause the public to suffer any additional burden of taxation through neglect on the part of the Administration, and, as I see it, that would be the only effect of our refusing to ' permit the Government to make the change desired in a matter of procedure.
There might be one other consequence. Our action in refusing to make the change suggested would be deliberately misinterpreted throughout the country; the people would be led to believe that in some way the Opposition were averse to allowing an expression of opinion within a certain time on a matter of public interest. We certainly desire to give every opportunity for an expression of opinion to any part of the community on a matter of public interest. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is not our intention to oppose this resolution.
One point that I wish to make perfectly clear, however, is this: We would not for one moment consent to the motion of my right hon. friend if in any way our action in so doing were likely to be interpreted as being prejudicial to the force of the amendment that is before the House at the present time, and which declares want of confidence in the Government as the view held by hon. gentlemen sitting on this side. With the distinct understanding, therefore, that our action in consenting to allow my right hon. friend to proceed will not in any way be construed, either in the House or out of it, as prejudicing the force of the motion of want of confidence in the Government which is now before the Chamber I am quite agreeable that my right hon. friend's motion shall pass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to say a word
anent the remarks of the hon. the leader of the Opposition before the motion carries, Mr. Speaker. I thought I had made it very clear when I first moved the motion that the reason the motion intervenes and that this Bill is necessary is not because
16i
the previous Act was insufficient in the circumstances, but that until at the very eve of the passing of the Act or just afterwards it had not been called to the attention of the Government that were a plebiscite to be held in the year 1920 there woulf be this extensive disfranchisement of the soldiers. It is because that circumstance was brought to the attention of the Government, and for that reason alone, that the postponement took place, and it is in order to save expense in providing a new list that this Bill is introduced. There is nothing extraordinary about it at all.
I understand that the leader of the Opposition asks from me a covenant that his acceding to this motion-which, by the way is not necessary, unless his acceding to it would be required to obtain a majority of Parliament, which I think far from likely *-shall not be construed as detracting from the force of the amendment now being pressed by the Opposition. I have never been able to see how his acceding to this motion could affect the force of the amendment-if it has any force. Certainly I do not intend to use it as detracting from the force of the amendment because I do not think it does detract, and, in fact, I never thought the amendment had very much force to begin with. We all know why the amendment was moved, and I do not think the country is going to be misled because we now interrupt the proceedings to take care of some useful matter of legislation. The country is 'not going to be misled by that consideration from fully grasping what the entire idea of the amendment before the House is, namely, to try to group a body of different opinions which cannot be grouped except under an amendment that calls for their being in power instead of us.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FEILDING (Shelburne and Queens) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the intimation of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) that the Government rushed the Franchise Bill through last session without knowing what they were doing is one which we should all be ready to accept. There is a point, however, to which I would like to draw attention. If this is a purely formal, non-contentious matter, I do not see any reason why we should not allow the motion to be made, although it is a very unusual departure from the customary procedure. But I notice in the morning papers a telegram from Toronto-and I may say that I have no in-4 p.m. terest in the Bill one way or the other-that the Bill which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) is intro-

during, is objected to by the temperance people of the country. If we are going to set aside the debate on the address to start a wrangle on this Bill, I question the wisdom of such a course; but if the Bill is purely non-contentious, I quite see the reason for making good the blunders of my right hon. friend, and we are ready to do so.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Hon. Hugh Guthrie (Solicitor General) Bill No. 2 to amend the Dominion Elections Act, was read tjie second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Ontario: Canada Temperance Act vote:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think, Mr. Chairman, before you take up the sub-sections I will ask that the Committee do now rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again to-morrow, I take this course because an amendment will have to be made to the Bill as it has passed the Senate, this amendment being requested by the various parties interested, and I think they are all agreed upon it.
By whom?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: By the parties who are asking that the amendment should be made.
What parties?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

One is the Ontario
Referendum Committee, the other is the Liberty League; I think those are the only two. I believe the amendment that they propose is merely one which goes to the appointment of scrutineers, and there will be agreement on it; but the amendment has not yet been received by me, and I would therefore ask that the Committee now report progress and ask leave to sit again to-morrow.	,
